strengths: The framework addresses a practically important video-editing problem with a coherent combination of user-controlled 3D placement, occlusion-aware masks, first-frame guidance, and video diffusion. The illustrated results show promising object fidelity and preservation of foreground occluders.

Reversing ROSE’s object-removal pairs provides a sensible source of supervision for insertion-induced shadows and illumination changes. Generating clean reference images from multiple object views is a useful dataset adaptation.

Table 1 reports substantial object-fidelity gains over the evaluated commercial tools: CLIP-I improves from Kling’s 0.6349 to 0.8122, and DINO-I from 0.5028 to 0.5678. Supplementary ablations support benefits from first-frame guidance and fine-tuning, while the 20-participant study provides complementary perceptual evidence.
The supplement provides useful training details, including the backbone, LoRA rank, learning rate, training duration, resolution, and inference steps.
weaknesses: The comparative evidence is insufficient for the claimed superiority over existing research. Only Pika-Pro and Kling are evaluated, despite discussing directly relevant methods such as VideoAnydoor, INVI, and GenProp. Moreover, commercial baselines receive textual placement instructions while the proposed method receives explicit geometric placement. These comparisons demonstrate a useful workflow advantage but do not isolate improvements over research methods under comparable spatial guidance.

Core technical details are underspecified. Section 3.2 does not adequately define visibility testing against scene geometry, lifting optical flow into a common 3D coordinate frame, neighbor selection and tracking, or handling occluded neighbors. Equation (2) uses the optical-flow notation for a 3D update and does not clearly express the stated average centroid translation. Translation alone also cannot capture rotations of a supporting surface. These omissions matter because reliable geometric propagation is a central contribution.

The claimed extension enabling edits outside the object mask is not described sufficiently to reproduce. Section 3.4 largely specifies LoRA fine-tuning of VACE, without clearly defining the training objective, spatial loss support, conditioning construction, or any architectural change responsible for surrounding illumination edits. This also leaves the algorithmic novelty beyond integrating established components unclear; no contribution type is explicitly declared, so I assess it as Algorithms/General.

The evaluation only partially measures the central claims. Generic VBench consistency scores do not directly establish correct visibility, placement, source-background preservation, or illumination. The implementation and interpretation of the reported Multi-View Consistency metric are insufficiently specified. There are no quantitative mask/occlusion accuracy measurements, and scene-flow propagation is assessed only qualitatively. Several gains over Kling are small, motion smoothness is lower, and uncertainty estimates are absent.

Dataset reproducibility is limited. ROSE++ lacks reported size, splits, category coverage, filtering statistics, and a precise image-generation model/version; citing the GPT-4 technical report does not identify the image generator. The numbers of sampled frames and generated candidates are unspecified. VOIBench’s video and object provenance, selection protocol, and availability are also unclear.

The production-readiness claims exceed the supplied evidence. Evaluation covers 50 scenes with two object insertions each, and the user study uses only 10% of the test videos. There is no systematic failure analysis, inference runtime, interaction-cost measurement, or robustness assessment under reconstruction errors, substantial support rotation, and prolonged occlusion. The results support a promising prototype, but these gaps and the missing research comparisons leave important concerns unresolved.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer vision problem: controllable video object insertion with occlusions and illumination changes. Combining explicit scene geometry with diffusion-based synthesis is a sensible approach, and the placement interface provides useful spatial control.

The reported results show meaningful object-fidelity improvements over the evaluated commercial tools. Table 1 reports CLIP-I/DINO-I of 0.8122/0.5678 versus Kling's 0.6349/0.5028, and the qualitative examples illustrate better placement and preservation of foreground occluders.

Reusing ROSE's paired renders for insertion supervision is practical and preserves supervision for object-induced shadows and reflections. The paper appropriately attributes the underlying dataset and pretrained components.

The supplementary material strengthens the evidence with quantitative component ablations, training settings, and a randomized-order user study with 20 participants. Table 3 supports benefits from first-frame conditioning and ROSE++ fine-tuning, while Table 4 reports strong preferences for the proposed system.
weaknesses: The comparative evaluation does not establish the claimed advantage over existing research methods. Only Pika-Pro and Kling are evaluated, despite discussing relevant approaches such as VideoAnydoor, GenProp, and InVi. Moreover, the proposed system receives precise manual 3D placement, whereas the commercial baselines receive relatively broad textual placement instructions. These comparisons demonstrate a useful workflow advantage but do not isolate improvements in insertion quality under comparable control.

Important technical details of the central geometry module are missing. Section 3.2.3 does not specify how optical flow is lifted into a common 3D coordinate system, how neighboring points are tracked or refreshed, or how occluded and unreliable correspondences are handled. The prose describes an averaged centroid translation, whereas Eq. (2) applies a pointwise flow field. Section 3.2.4 asserts visibility-aware rasterization without specifying the depth comparison and visibility rules. These omissions hinder reproduction and assessment of the claimed occlusion robustness.

The evidence only partially tests the principal claims. Generic VBench consistency scores do not directly establish correct occlusion ordering, accurate placement, or physically consistent lighting. The implementation and interpretation of 'Multi-View Consistency' are insufficiently specified. Scene-flow propagation is supported by one qualitative example, and lighting improvements are illustrated without targeted quantitative evaluation. Table 3's geometry-only improvement is modest and reduces reference-image similarity, warranting a more direct geometry evaluation.

ROSE++ and VOIBench are insufficiently documented. The manuscript omits ROSE++ size, filtering and split details, candidate-generation counts, and the exact image-generation model/version; citing the GPT-4 technical report does not identify a reproducible image-generation system. VOIBench's video provenance, selection criteria, annotations, and relationship to training data are also unclear. The supplement supplies useful optimization settings but does not resolve these dataset-level gaps.

The algorithmic contribution remains insufficiently distinguished from its established components: Uni4D reconstruction, single-view object reconstruction, flow-based propagation, SAM2, first-frame inpainting, and VACE LoRA adaptation. Such integration can be valuable, but stronger matched baselines and targeted ablations are needed to establish its scientific contribution. In particular, Table 2's single consistency score does not establish the proposed explanation that generated references prevent copy-and-paste overfitting.

Claims of production suitability and significant superiority exceed the available evidence. Evaluation covers 50 source clips with two object choices each, the user study covers only 10% of test videos, and uncertainty is not reported. Some gains over Kling are small, and Kling scores higher on motion smoothness. End-to-end runtime, manual placement effort, failure rates, and robustness to reconstruction errors, full occlusion, and rotating supports are not evaluated. The promising demonstrations therefore support a narrower claim than reliable production deployment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important video-editing problem: controllable object insertion with consistent placement, occlusions, and lighting. The integration of explicit scene geometry with diffusion generation is well motivated and offers a useful practical contribution.

ROSE++ provides a sensible supervision strategy by reversing object-removal pairs that include shadows and reflections. Adding generated reference images makes these pairs usable for reference-conditioned insertion while retaining supervision for effects outside the object mask.

Results against the evaluated commercial tools are promising. Table 1 reports substantial reference-fidelity gains over Kling, including CLIP-I of 0.8122 versus 0.6349 and DINO-I of 0.5678 versus 0.5028. The illustrated examples also show improved placement and preservation of occluding scene elements.

The supplementary material strengthens the evidence with component ablations and a randomized user study involving 20 participants. The reported 70% preference for overall naturalness and 86.67% for occlusion integrity support the perceptual advantages within the evaluated comparison.
The paper attributes its major pretrained components and provides useful implementation details, including the backbone, LoRA rank, training duration, resolution, and inference steps.
weaknesses: The main comparison excludes relevant research methods discussed in the paper, including VideoAnyDoor, GenProp, and INVI. Comparisons only against Pika-Pro and Kling do not establish the claimed advantage over existing research. Furthermore, these tools receive text-based placement instructions while InsertAnywhere receives explicit geometric placement and mask guidance. This is a useful comparison of complete workflows, but it does not isolate the proposed technical advances. A strong research baseline with comparable spatial or first-frame conditioning is needed.

Several central implementation details remain underspecified. Section 3.2 does not adequately explain flow lifting, neighborhood tracking, visibility testing, or SAM2 prompting. Equation (2) applies a spatially varying flow to each object point, whereas the text describes updating the centroid with an averaged displacement. Section 3.4 does not specify the training objective, LoRA target layers, or precisely how conditioning permits edits outside the mask. These omissions materially affect reproducibility.

ROSE++ lacks basic dataset documentation: its size, retained examples, scene/object distribution, splits, filtering, and generation counts are not reported. The image-generating VLM is cited only through the GPT-4 technical report, which does not identify the actual image-generation model or version. VOIBench also lacks sufficiently detailed provenance and selection criteria. These gaps make the data contribution and evaluation coverage difficult to assess.

The metrics provide limited direct evidence for the central geometry and illumination claims. Background temporal consistency does not establish preservation of the input background, and the implementation of the reported multi-view consistency metric is insufficiently explained. There are no direct mask-accuracy, occlusion-ordering, placement, or shadow-fidelity measurements. Table 3 shows only modest generic-metric improvements from geometry-aware masks, alongside reduced reference similarity; it therefore does not conclusively establish the claimed geometric benefit.

The production-readiness claim exceeds the demonstrated scope. Evaluation covers 50 source clips and two objects per clip, with the user study restricted to 10% of the test set and no uncertainty estimates. End-to-end runtime, interaction effort, failure rates, and reconstruction sensitivity are not reported. Averaged local scene flow also does not establish support for rotating supports or more complex interactions. The promising integration and examples make this a close decision, but the missing research comparisons and incomplete validation leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important video-editing problem: combining controllable placement, dynamic occlusion handling, and optical effects outside the object mask. The integration of reconstructed geometry with generative synthesis is practically relevant, and the qualitative examples show promising results.

Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is a well-motivated contribution. Table 4 provides direct supporting evidence: alignment improves optics-region PSNR from 19.91 to 27.24 dB on 25 held-out examples, while unedited-region PSNR remains essentially unchanged.

The experimental evaluation includes several useful controls: VACE receives the proposed masks and the same edited first frame, additional variants are fine-tuned on ROSE++, and component ablations distinguish first-frame anchoring, fine-tuning, and alignment. The full method leads five of six metrics in Table 1.

The supplementary user studies complement automatic metrics. Strong preferences for object realism and overall naturalness support the practical value of the complete pipeline, while the additional study explicitly examines shadow- and reflection-rich scenes.

Reusing paired object-removal data for insertion supervision is sensible and appropriately attributed. The reference-image construction ablation supports the usefulness of ROSE++ beyond simply reversing source and target videos.
weaknesses: The geometric contribution is insufficiently validated relative to the claims. Equations (3)–(4) apply only an averaged translation, so they cannot make an object follow a rotating support's orientation. Nearest points can also span different moving surfaces. Figure 9 provides a qualitative example, but there is no quantitative placement, trajectory, mask-accuracy, or occlusion evaluation against simpler propagation alternatives. Claims of broadly reliable 4D placement therefore exceed the demonstrated evidence.

Important implementation details are missing. The paper does not specify the complete training objective, alignment weight and normalization, exact aligned layers, or which shared parameters are trainable. Stop-gradient prevents gradients through the teacher branch but does not make its features fixed across updates if its weights are shared and trained. The visibility/depth test, SAM 2 refinement procedure, KNN parameter, and propagation before an arbitrary anchor frame also need clarification.

The dataset contributions are inadequately documented. ROSE++ lacks a reported total size, scene/object statistics, detailed split policy, and evidence that the held-out samples exclude related training scenes or assets. VOIBench lacks source attribution, category counts, and clear accounting of insertion tasks per clip. The manuscript claims an open-source release but supplies no access information; the reference-image generator is identified only through a GPT-4 technical-report citation.

Evaluation does not fully isolate the claimed optical advance from simpler alternatives. The paired optics test is small and synthetic, with insufficient detail about masked metric computation and no uncertainty estimates. A dilation or predicted extended-mask baseline would test whether feature alignment is necessary. The real-video user studies favor the full pipeline, but omit the otherwise identical model without alignment, and lighting-preference margins over Kling are relatively modest.

Comparisons omit directly relevant insertion methods discussed in the paper, including VideoAnydoor, DreamInsert, and OmniInsert, without explaining their exclusion. The existing comparisons establish advantages over several general editing systems but leave competitiveness with specialized insertion approaches uncertain.

Several conclusions overstate what the evidence establishes: improved multi-view similarity does not prove that the network infers 4D geometry and lighting, attention visualizations do not establish physical correctness, and 'production-grade' guarantees are unsupported by robustness or failure-rate analysis. Overall, the promising empirical results make this a close decision, but the geometry-validation and reproducibility gaps favor borderline rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important video-editing problem: combining controllable placement and occlusion handling with shadows and reflections outside the object mask. The integration is practically relevant, and the illustrated results show promising improvements over the evaluated baselines.

Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is a plausible contribution: extended masks derived from paired training videos provide privileged supervision, while inference requires only the object mask. Table 4 provides direct supporting evidence: alignment improves optics-region PSNR from 19.91 to 27.24 dB, with corresponding LPIPS and SSIM improvements and approximately unchanged unedited-region PSNR.

The evaluation includes meaningful controls beyond comparisons with commercial systems. Table 2 evaluates VACE fine-tuned on the same dataset, Table 3 separates first-frame anchoring, fine-tuning, and alignment, and the supplement states that applicable baselines receive the same edited first frame.

The supplementary user studies strengthen the perceptual evidence. Overall naturalness receives 58.64% preference in the four-method study, and the optics-focused study includes a data-matched VACE baseline. These results complement the automatic metrics.

Reusing ROSE's paired renders for insertion supervision and constructing isolated reference images is a useful data contribution. The supplement also supplies training hardware, resolution, iteration count, LoRA rank, and inference costs.
weaknesses: The geometric contribution is insufficiently validated relative to its claims. Equations (3)–(4) propagate the object using an average translation of nearby scene points; they do not estimate support rotation or ensure that neighbors belong to the supporting surface. Figure 9 offers qualitative evidence, but there is no quantitative trajectory, mask, or occlusion evaluation against simpler propagation alternatives. Robustness to rotating supports, mixed foreground/background neighbors, and accumulated depth/flow errors remains unclear.

Important details of the central alignment method are missing. Equation (7) does not specify the complete training objective, alignment weight, feature normalization, or exact aligned layers. Stop-gradient prevents gradients through the teacher branch during that computation, but parameter sharing means the teacher is not fixed across optimization steps as claimed. These omissions impede reproduction and understanding of why alignment preserves useful optical information.

The optics evidence is encouraging but does not fully establish the proposed mechanism's necessity. There is no quantitative comparison against straightforward mask dilation or training with extended masks. The paired evaluation uses only 25 held-out ROSE++ samples, without uncertainty estimates or a clear account of scene/object separation. The optics-focused user study compares complete systems rather than directly comparing the model with and without alignment.

Evaluation coverage and specification remain incomplete. Closely related insertion methods discussed in the paper, including VideoAnyDoor, DreamInsert, and OmniInsert, are not evaluated or given explicit exclusion rationales. VOIBench lacks detailed provenance, category counts, and placement/annotation protocols; the reported multi-view consistency metric is not operationally defined. Consequently, the breadth of the claimed advantage is difficult to assess.

Dataset reproducibility is limited: the manuscript does not report ROSE++'s size, detailed splits, candidate-generation count, exact image-editing model/version, or numerical extended-mask thresholds. The generic GPT-4 technical-report citation does not identify the image-generation system. Claims that the method guarantees photorealistic rendering or achieves production-grade quality also exceed the demonstrated evidence. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the promising optics results make this a close decision, but the methodological omissions and limited geometric validation favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: inserting reference objects into videos while preserving placement, occlusions, appearance, and surrounding optical effects. The integration of geometric mask propagation with optics-aware synthesis is coherent and practically motivated.

Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is a promising contribution: training with extended-mask features provides privileged supervision while requiring only an object mask at inference. Table 4 offers direct supporting evidence, with optics-region PSNR improving from 19.91 to 27.24 dB over the model without alignment, while unedited-region PSNR remains essentially unchanged.

The evaluation includes meaningful controls beyond comparisons with commercial tools. Table 2 evaluates VACE fine-tuned on ROSE++ using the proposed masks, and Table 3 separates first-frame anchoring, fine-tuning, and alignment. The full system leads on five of six reported metrics in Table 1.

The supplementary user studies complement the automated metrics. Overall-naturalness preference reaches 58.64% in the general study, and the optics-focused study includes a data-matched VACE baseline. The qualitative examples support improved handling of occlusions and surrounding shadows.

ROSE++ is a useful adaptation of an attributed existing dataset, adding reference images for insertion supervision. The supplement provides training hardware, iteration count, LoRA rank, resolution, and inference costs. Taken together, the contributions support a slight preference for acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: Geometric robustness is less convincingly established than synthesis quality. Equations (3)–(4) propagate objects using an average translation of nearby scene points; they cannot follow support-surface rotation and can mix motions from different surfaces. Figure 9 provides a useful example, but there is no quantitative placement, tracking, or occlusion-accuracy evaluation, nor comparison with simpler propagation alternatives. The broad claims of guaranteed geometric consistency and production-grade behavior exceed this evidence.

Important implementation details are missing for the central alignment method: the complete training objective, alignment weight and normalization, selected feature layers, and whether the two branches share diffusion noise and timesteps. Stop-gradient blocks gradients through the teacher branch but does not make its shared parameters fixed across optimization steps, so the teacher description is imprecise. Visibility testing against scene geometry and SAM 2 refinement also need clearer specification.

The dataset contributions are insufficiently documented. ROSE++ lacks a reported total size, detailed split construction, scene/object overlap analysis, and reference-generation acceptance statistics. The image-editing model is cited through the GPT-4 technical report rather than an identifiable image-generation version. VOIBench lacks detailed provenance, category counts, and redistribution information, limiting reproducibility and assessment of coverage.

The experimental configurations need reconciliation. Supplement D states that VACE receives the same edited first frame as the proposed method, but Table 3's configuration (b), apparently the corresponding mask-plus-first-frame setup without fine-tuning, differs substantially from the VACE baseline in Table 1. Likewise, the relationship between fine-tuned VACE in Table 2 and configuration (c) is unclear. These differences weaken attribution of the gains until the exact conditioning and training settings are specified.

Some evaluation claims are stronger than the measurements justify. VBench background consistency does not directly establish preservation relative to the source, and the multi-view consistency metric is insufficiently defined. Paired optical evaluation uses only 25 held-out synthetic samples; uncertainty estimates and scene-stratified results are absent. User-study lighting preferences are encouraging but comparatively modest, and neither attention visualizations nor reference-consistency improvements establish physical correctness of the generated lighting.
